questions.prompt: A team commits a secret-scanning script to `hooks/pre-commit` in the repository. A new engineer clones the repository and commits an AWS key without any warning. Why?
choices: The script needs to be signed before Git trusts it
Git looks for hooks in `.git/hooks/` (or `core.hooksPath`), which `git clone` never populates; each clone has to install the hooks or set `core.hooksPath` itself
Hooks only run on the default branch
The engineer's Git version is too old to run hooks
questions.explanation: Hooks are not part of what Git clones, for security reasons: a clone must never run code it just downloaded. A versioned hooks directory still needs `git config core.hooksPath` or a framework's install command in every clone, which is why client hooks cannot be the enforcement.

questions.prompt: You staged a fix in `app.py` and kept a second, unfinished edit in the same file unstaged. Your pre-commit hook runs a linter on `app.py` as it is on disk. What is wrong with that?
choices: Nothing: the file on disk is what will be committed
Linters cannot read files that have unstaged changes
The hook also stages the unfinished edit

The commit is made from the index, so the linter checks a version that will not be committed; a framework sets the unstaged edits aside as a patch, runs the hook on the staged content and re-applies the patch
questions.explanation: `git commit` writes the index as a tree. With a partially staged file, the disk holds staged plus unstaged content. pre-commit and minihooks run `git diff-index --binary $(git write-tree)`, check out the index, run the hooks and `git apply` the patch afterwards.

questions.prompt: A whitespace-trimming hook rewrites a staged file and exits 0. What does the pre-commit framework do, and why?
choices: It fails the hook because the file changed, leaves the fix unstaged and stops the commit, so the user reviews the change and stages it
It passes the hook because the exit code is 0
It stages the fix automatically and lets the commit proceed
It reverts the fix and passes the hook
questions.explanation: The framework compares the working tree before and after each hook; a change is a failure regardless of the exit code. Staging fixes silently would commit content nobody looked at. lefthook's `stage_fixed: true` is a deliberate opt-in to the other policy.

questions.prompt: Three hooks are configured in this order: a fixer on `*.py`, a checker on `*.json`, and a secret scanner on all text files. Which may run at the same time without changing any result?
choices: All three, because hooks are independent programs
None; hooks must always run one after another
The fixer and the JSON checker, whose file sets are disjoint; the scanner must wait for both, because it reads files the fixer may change
The scanner and the fixer, because the scanner only reads
questions.explanation: Two hooks interfere only through shared files. A hook depends on every earlier hook whose file set overlaps its own (or that may touch anything), which keeps configuration order where order matters and runs the rest in parallel.

questions.prompt: Your bare repository's `pre-receive` hook rejects a push because one of five new commits adds a 40 MB file. What does the server keep from that push?
choices: The four commits that passed, on the target branch
Nothing: the objects were received into a quarantine directory, the hook's non-zero exit declined every ref in the push, and the quarantine was deleted
All objects, but no refs move until `git gc` runs
The commits, on a hidden ref the pusher can retry from
questions.explanation: `pre-receive` decides for the whole push at once. Git receives the pack into a quarantine object directory that the hook's own `git` commands can read; only on exit 0 are the objects moved into the repository and the refs updated. `update` is the per-ref hook if you need partial acceptance.

questions.prompt: The team wants Conventional Commit messages and no secrets on `main`. Which setup actually guarantees it?
choices: A `commit-msg` hook and a secret-scanning `pre-commit` hook in every developer's clone
A `.pre-commit-config.yaml` in the repository
A wiki page and code review
Client hooks for fast feedback, plus the same checks in a required CI job and a server-side `pre-receive` hook or hosted push rules, because client hooks can be missing or skipped with `--no-verify`
questions.explanation: Client hooks are advisory: they are not cloned, `--no-verify` skips them, and web edits never see them. Only checks that run where the developer has no control, on the server and in required CI, hold as policy; client hooks make the same feedback arrive seconds after the mistake.
